speaker: Albert Gu
title: No Priors Ep. 70 | With Cartesia Co-Founders Karan Goel & Albert Gu
question: In AI research, why do Transformers often underperform when applied directly to raw perceptual signals like audio waveforms or pixels despite seeming universal on text?
guest: Every token in text already has a meaning; it's very dense information. Now, if you look at a video or an audio signal, it's highly compressible. If you sample at a really high rate, it's very continuous, and that means it's compressible. Different types of models just have different inductive biases or strengths at modeling these things. The first types of models we were looking at were really good at modeling raw waveforms, raw pixels, things like that, but not as good at modeling text, where Transformers are way better. One thing we learned is that in general there's no free lunch there. People think that you can throw a Transformer at anything and it just works. Actually, it doesn't really. If you try to throw it at the raw pixel level or the raw sample level in audio waveforms, it doesn't work nearly as well. Transformers have really evolved hand-in-hand with the whole ecosystem of the training pipeline, so the places people use Transformers, the data has already been processed in a way that helps the model—for example, tokenization. When you break away from those assumptions, some of your modeling assumptions no longer hold, and other models actually work better.

points.core: Transformers co-evolved with preprocessing pipelines like tokenization that pre-compress text data.
points.note: Accept: Transformers rely on ecosystem preprocessing (e.g., BPE/tokenizers) tailored to their assumptions; text is already pre-compressed before entering the model. Do not credit: generic claims that Transformers are slow or need lots of data without citing pipeline/tokenization co-evolution.

points.core: Raw perceptual signals are continuous, highly compressible streams unlike information-dense text tokens.
points.note: Accept: raw audio, video, or pixels are high-sample-rate, continuous, redundant, or low information density per sample compared to dense text tokens. Do not credit: vague statements that audio or video are "harder" without contrasting continuity/compressibility against density.

points.core: Breaking those preprocessing assumptions invalidates the Transformer's inductive bias on raw inputs.
points.note: Accept: removing pre-compression/tokenization breaks the modeling assumptions Transformers depend on, causing alternative architectures with different inductive biases to outperform. Do not credit: claiming Transformers only fail because of quadratic memory/compute limits without mentioning inductive bias or modeling fit.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Transformers work well on text largely because text arrives pre-digested: tokens are discrete, semantically dense, and already compressed by human language, so each position carries meaningful information and sequences stay short. Raw perceptual signals are the opposite, and three problems follow.

First, sequence length. A second of audio is 16,000+ samples and a modest image is tens of thousands of pixels; self-attention's cost grows quadratically, so modelling useful context becomes prohibitively expensive.

Second, low information density. Individual samples or pixels are highly redundant, noisy, and nearly meaningless alone. The model spends capacity on fine-grained local correlations and imperceptible detail rather than the long-range, abstract structure attention is good at.

Third, weak inductive bias. Transformers lack the built-in locality, translation equivariance, and multi-scale hierarchy of convolutions, so they must learn these from data, which makes them data-hungry and prone to underperforming at smaller scales (as the original ViT paper found).

This is why practical systems insert a tokenisation or compression step first, such as image patches, spectrograms, convolutional front-ends, or learned codecs (VQ-VAE, EnCodec, latent diffusion). Given enough data and compute, the gap narrows, but the efficiency penalty remains.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Transformers excel on text because words and subwords are discrete, semantically dense symbols already compressed by human language. In contrast, raw pixels and audio waveforms are continuous, high-frequency signals with massive local redundancy and almost no semantic meaning at the individual sample level. Applying self-attention directly to raw perceptual inputs creates two fundamental bottlenecks: computational intractability and weak inductive bias. Because standard self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, flattening an image into millions of pixels or a few seconds of audio into tens of thousands of waveform samples makes global attention prohibitively expensive while diluting attention weights across low-level noise and fine-grained correlations. Furthermore, unlike convolutional networks or structured state-space models, vanilla Transformers lack built-in priors for spatial and temporal locality, translation equivariance, and multiscale hierarchy, forcing them to inefficiently learn basic signal processing from vast amounts of data. Consequently, perceptual Transformers generally succeed only after compressing raw signals into coarser, higher-level units—such as image patches, spectrograms, or learned latent tokens—that restore text-like information density.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Transformers look universal on text mostly because text arrives already compressed. Words and subword tokens are dense, meaningful, human-made symbols, so each token carries a lot of information and sequences stay fairly short.

Raw perceptual signals are the opposite. One second of audio holds about 16,000 to 48,000 samples, and an image holds millions of pixel values. Each individual value means almost nothing alone, and the meaning comes from local patterns spread across many of them. Self-attention's cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so attending over raw samples quickly becomes too expensive in compute and memory. Most of that capacity also goes to modeling low-level redundancy and noise instead of structure.

Transformers also lack the built-in assumptions, called inductive biases, that suit signals. Convolutions assume locality and translation equivariance, and Transformers don't. Without those assumptions they need much more data to learn the same regularities.

So in practice people add a "tokenizer" in front of the Transformer. Examples are ViT's image patches, wav2vec's convolutional front-end, neural audio codecs like EnCodec, and VQ-VAE latents. These compress the signal into shorter, more meaningful units, which recreates the conditions that make Transformers work well on language.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Transformers excel on text because subword tokens are already discrete, compressed, semantically rich units. Raw perceptual signals like pixels or audio waveforms lack this structure, creating three fundamental bottlenecks for vanilla self-attention. First, raw signals are extremely long and dense—even a modest image or a few seconds of audio contains tens of thousands of elements—making self-attention's quadratic memory and compute scaling prohibitive. Second, individual pixels or waveform samples have very low semantic density and high local redundancy; attention wastes capacity modeling fine-grained noise and neighboring correlations rather than high-level patterns. Third, Transformers possess weak perceptual inductive biases: unlike convolutional networks, they lack built-in locality, translation equivariance, and hierarchical multi-scale processing, so learning basic spatial or temporal structure directly from raw inputs requires vastly more data and compute. Consequently, vision and audio Transformers typically rely on frontends—such as patch embeddings, convolutional stems, spectrograms, or neural codecs—to compress raw signals into shorter, more meaningful token sequences before applying attention.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Transformers can learn from raw pixels or audio samples, but treating each pixel or sample as a token makes learning expensive. Text tokenization already gives the model discrete, reusable units such as words and word pieces. A single pixel or audio sample carries little meaning on its own. Useful features such as edges and harmonics emerge from patterns across nearby samples.

Raw signals also produce much longer sequences, and standard self-attention compares every token with every other token, so its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. A vanilla Transformer can learn spatial or temporal patterns, but it lacks the built-in bias of a convolution to look for the same local pattern at different positions. That can make it less data-efficient.

Many successful vision and audio Transformers therefore group pixels into patches or use a learned front end to turn waveforms into shorter sequences of features. The Transformer can then spend more of its capacity modeling relationships among those features.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A text Transformer usually starts with tokens, not raw sensory data. A tokenizer has already grouped characters into recurring units such as words or word fragments. An individual pixel or audio sample carries much less information on its own. Edges emerge from relationships among neighboring pixels, and sounds take shape across many samples.

A standard Transformer can learn those relationships, but it has little built-in preference for nearby inputs or for recognizing the same pattern at different positions. It must learn that structure from data. Raw inputs also produce long sequences, and the cost of standard self-attention grows quadratically with sequence length.

This is mainly a matter of data and compute efficiency. Image patches, spectrograms, and learned convolutional front ends can give attention a shorter sequence of more informative units, making it easier to learn how those units relate across space or time.
